sections.name: TextEdit, Bullet, Presentation, textOf, TableSpec
sections.title: Shared types and bullet reader
sections.what: Defines the shape of a text edit and of a presentation. It also includes a small helper that reads the text of a bullet, whether the bullet is stored as plain text or as an object.
sections.why: Names the shapes once so the rest of the file can use them consistently.
sections.watch_out: A bullet can be plain text or an object, so any new code must handle both forms.

sections.name: readTableSpec
sections.title: Table layout check
sections.what: Confirms that a saved table is valid. It allows two to five columns, rows that reference every text element exactly once and in order, and optional column widths that are positive. It throws a clear error when the table is invalid and returns the table when it is valid.
sections.why: Stops an edit or a saved page from producing a table that cannot be drawn or read correctly.
sections.watch_out: It returns nothing when no table is saved, so callers must handle that case.

sections.name: applyPresentationEdits
sections.title: Applying edits and enforcing limits
sections.what: Applies each wording change to a copy, enforces the length limits and the page text budget, and records the old wording. It also marks the slide as user-edited and pinned.
sections.why: Likely reason: the wording rules and the change record must live in one place so every save path enforces the same limits.
sections.watch_out: The text budget is checked only after all edits in the loop, so a single edit can be accepted at first and judged against the whole slide's total later.

summary: Checks a user's wording changes to a saved slide presentation and applies them to a copy, recording the old wording, without changing the underlying facts.
purpose: Gives one shared set of rules for accepting edited slide text, so saving, replaying and exporting all agree on what is allowed.
why: The header says this is a pure wording policy shared by native saves, prepared replay and export. Likely reason it is kept free of side effects: the same rules run in several places and must not disagree.
how: First makes a full copy of the presentation so the original is untouched. For each edit, it finds the slide and the target (title, subtitle, or a bullet named bullet-N), rejects unknown targets, and checks length limits. It then writes the new text, saves the previous text in the slide's metadata, adds a footnote saying the wording is not source-verified, and flags any linked citation as no longer verified. After all edits, it checks the total text on each edited slide against a budget, marks the slides as pinned, and returns the new copy with a list of changes.
inputs: The original presentation, and a list of edits. Each edit names a slide, a text element, and the new text. If the slide has a table, its layout is read from the slide metadata.
outputs: A new presentation object (called recipe) and a history list. Each history entry holds the edit and the text it replaced. If a rule fails, the function throws an error with a plain message.
risks: Edited wording passes these checks without being verified against sources. The footnote and citation warning are the only protection against that. Table rules apply only when a table is saved on the slide. The rules assume the slide metadata has the expected shape, and that shape is not documented in this file.
debug: If a save fails with a length message, check the title and subtitle limits here and the textBudget value in the slide metadata, which must be a whole number from 900 to 1800. If a table edit is rejected, check that the table rows point to every text element exactly once and in order, as readTableSpec enforces. If an edit is rejected as missing, check that the element id is title, subtitle, or bullet-N with N in range. If the change history looks wrong, check how the before value is chosen.
